---
title: "Opposing criterion directions"
subtitle: "4.2 · after the postrank theory book, ch. 12 and 19"
description: "Comparison of directional disagreement, posterior uncertainty and isolated-pair expected costs."
---

Criteria can support opposite directions for a given pair. The matrix identifies these disagreements by comparing
forward and reverse error probabilities on each criterion. The bars evaluate the weighted costs of both strict
directions and withholding. Supplied normal posteriors and finite known-state examples distinguish disagreement
within a state from uncertainty about that state. The smaller posterior expected directional cost can reflect both
sources, and is therefore not generally a measure of criterion conflict alone. A complete coherent report imposes
constraints beyond this isolated-pair comparison.

## Numerical illustrations {#what-to-try}

- **Six sites, B–C.** The equal-weight costs are .4841 for B above C and .5159 for C above B. The map has 3
  opposing pairs. Withholding is cheaper for this pair on its own, but these actions do not yet form a common grade.
- **Thirty sites.** There are 397 opposing pairs. For the selected pair, the smaller expected directional cost is
  .3652. Each criterion has equal error weight; the table keeps its separate errors visible.
- **Certain opposition.** The two directions each cost .5000; withholding costs .2000. Here the smaller directional
  cost is also the statewise conflict quantity. The additional boundary preset shows every action sharing the
  minimum when withholding has the same cost.
- **Uncertain agreement.** The smaller posterior directional cost is still .5000, but statewise γ is .0000 in each
  state. The criteria agree within every state; uncertainty about which state holds creates the directional cost.
- **Zero error weight.** The opposing pair stays on the map, while its cheaper direction costs .0000 and the
  reverse costs 1.0000. A disagreement on a criterion with zero weight does not itself force weighted error.
- **Latent equality.** One criterion’s reverse errors are .600 and .900, both above one half, yet it prefers the
  smaller one. The other criterion prefers the opposite direction. Both weighted directions cost .7500; comparing
  errors with their reverse detects this disagreement even with equality mass.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
A strict direction counts as wrong at equality. The map compares forward and reverse errors on every criterion;
it does not use a one-half threshold or discard criteria with zero weight. Statewise γ excludes withholding.
Posterior uncertainty and substantive conflict need not have a unique additive decomposition. A full coherent
report can choose differently from an isolated pair.
:::

library(postrank)
